reference.source: AAO-HNS clinical practice guideline and Bárány Society diagnostic criteria for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
clinicalPearls: The commonest cause of recurrent positional vertigo, produced by displaced utricular otoconia entering a semicircular canal; brief spinning is triggered by changes in head position relative to gravity such as lying down, rolling over in bed, or looking up.
The posterior semicircular canal is affected in the large majority of cases; individual attacks are brief, typically settling within a minute even if the provoking position is maintained.

The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre is diagnostic for posterior canal disease, provoking an upbeating torsional nystagmus with a short latency, a crescendo-decrescendo time course, and fatigability on repetition.

Horizontal (lateral) canal involvement is identified with the supine roll (Pagnini-McClure) test, producing a horizontal nystagmus that is geotropic in canalithiasis and apogeotropic in cupulolithiasis.

Canalithiasis (free-floating debris within the canal) and cupulolithiasis (debris adherent to the cupula) generate different nystagmus latencies and durations and guide the choice of repositioning manoeuvre.

Treatment is with canalith repositioning: the Epley or Semont manoeuvre for the posterior canal, and the Lempert (barbecue) roll or Gufoni manoeuvre for the horizontal canal; medication has little role.
Secondary BPPV follows head trauma, vestibular neuritis, prolonged recumbency, inner-ear surgery, and ageing, and is associated with reduced vitamin D and osteopenia; these cases recur more often.
The direction and plane of the nystagmus localise the affected canal — posterior (upbeat-torsional), horizontal (geotropic or apogeotropic), and the rare anterior canal (predominantly downbeat).
reference.pathophysiology: Otoconia — calcium carbonate crystals normally embedded in the utricular macula — become dislodged and migrate into one of the semicircular canals, most often the gravity-dependent posterior canal. In canalithiasis the free-floating particles move under gravity when the head is repositioned, dragging endolymph and deflecting the cupula abnormally, which generates a transient sensation of rotation and a characteristic nystagmus with latency and fatigability. In cupulolithiasis the particles adhere to the cupula itself, rendering it gravity-sensitive and producing a more immediate and persistent deflection. The resulting inappropriate canal signal conflicts with the otolith and visual inputs, giving rise to vertigo. Degeneration and demineralisation of otoconia with age, trauma, ischaemia, and other inner-ear disease predispose to their detachment.
additionalDifferentials: central positional vertigo or nystagmus from posterior fossa or craniocervical junction lesions
vestibular neuritis in the acute phase
additionalInvestigations: Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre for posterior and anterior canal disease
supine roll (Pagnini-McClure) test for horizontal canal disease
video-nystagmography or Frenzel goggles to remove visual fixation and characterise nystagmus
pure-tone audiometry when there are cochlear symptoms
MRI of the brain when central features are present or the presentation is atypical
serum vitamin D and orthostatic blood pressure in recurrent or secondary cases
redFlags: positional nystagmus that is purely downbeat, direction-changing, or does not fit a single canal plane, suggesting a central lesion
positional nystagmus lacking latency, adaptation, or fatigability
associated neurological signs, intractable vomiting, or imbalance out of proportion to the vertigo
new-onset severe headache or occipital pain with positional symptoms
sensorineural hearing loss developing alongside the positional vertigo
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent, with most patients responding to a single or small number of repositioning manoeuvres and many resolving spontaneously; recurrence is common, affecting a substantial minority within a few years, particularly in secondary and idiopathic elderly cases.
pitfalls: mistaking central positional vertigo for BPPV and thereby overlooking posterior fossa pathology
omitting positional testing in a patient reporting positional dizziness
performing a repositioning manoeuvre for the wrong canal or the wrong side
concluding treatment has failed after a single manoeuvre without re-testing and repeating it
attributing chronic, non-positional dizziness to BPPV when persistent postural-perceptual dizziness or another disorder is responsible

management: Treat posterior canal disease with canalith repositioning manoeuvres such as the Epley or Semont
Treat horizontal canal disease with the Lempert (barbecue) roll or the Gufoni manoeuvre
Confirm the affected canal with the Dix-Hallpike and supine roll tests to direct the appropriate repositioning manoeuvre
Limit vestibular sedatives to brief symptom relief only, as they do not treat the otoconial displacement and impair central compensation
Teach home repositioning or Brandt-Daroff exercises for recurrent or residual symptoms
Reassess after treatment, repeating the manoeuvre for persistent nystagmus and investigating secondary causes such as vitamin D deficiency in recurrent disease
Refer for neuro-otology review and brain MRI if central features, atypical nystagmus or treatment resistance are present
